To use ponerse for quick changes of state (nervioso, rojo, contento).
To use volverse for changes of character, often unexpected.
To use hacerse for deliberate changes: profession, religion, ideology.
To use quedarse for the result of a situation (sin palabras, embarazada).
To use convertirse en and llegar a ser.
September. Ana has gone back to school. On Friday evening, the club in Madrid has a video call with her and Mihai. A few months have passed and everyone has changed a little.
Ana! You look lovely! You’ve got a tan.
I spent August by the Black Sea. And you? You look different.
I’ve become a vegetarian. I haven’t eaten meat since June.
And I got very sad when she told me. She was my best pork ramen customer!
Kenji has become very dramatic with age.
And you’ve become very serious since you started working at the bank. You don’t sing karaoke any more.
Well, I’ve turned into a responsible adult. From Monday to Friday, anyway.
And Mrs Suzuki? How is she?
Since she got back from Kyoto, she’s taken up Japanese painting. She says her husband, José, would have become a great painter and that she wants to finish what he started.
How lovely… Speaking of painters: Andrei, my pupil, has won a drawing competition for the whole of Romania.
The shy boy with the cats? No way!
The very same. When they gave him the prize, he went so red he looked like a tomato. But then he spoke in front of a hundred people. He’s become much more self-confident.
And Rosa Elena? Is she talking yet?
She’s eight months old, Kenji. But she gets furious if you take her dummy away. And when she sees Tama on the phone, she goes completely still, staring at her.
Well, Tama has become famous. Now she has an Instagram account with five thousand followers.
Really? The library cat has become a star!

1. Why so many verbs for “to become”?

English uses “get”, “become”, “go” and “turn”: get nervous, become a doctor, go mad, turn red. Spanish has even more, each with its own shade. The choice depends on three questions: is the change momentary or lasting? Is it deliberate or not? Is it good or bad?
en una estrella, en un adulto
after a long time and effort
Se puso nervioso en el examen.
Se ha vuelto muy nervioso con la edad.
Se puso triste al oír la noticia.
Desde el divorcio, se ha vuelto triste.
Me pongo rojo cuando hablo en público.
Test: could it be gone by tomorrow? If so, ponerse. If the person themselves has changed, volverse.
“Ponerse” is also used for the colour of skin and things: ponerse moreno (to get a tan), el cielo se puso gris.
My cousin became a doctor after ten years of study.
They became friends at the club.

“Quedarse embarazada” = to get pregnant (a set phrase). Not “ponerse embarazada”!
“Hacerse” shows the person played a part: se hizo rico (he worked for it). “Volverse rico” sounds more like luck or a sudden change.

The speech (translated into Spanish by Andrei himself) he gave at the prize-giving.
Good afternoon. A year ago, I was the quietest boy in the school. When a teacher asked me a question, I went red and couldn’t speak.
My parents were worried. My dad said I was becoming a strange boy. He wanted me to become an engineer, like him.
But then a Spanish teacher came along who didn’t ask me to speak. She asked me to draw. And little by little, my drawings became my words.
I don’t know if I’ll become a great artist. But I do know that I no longer keep quiet when I have something to say.
I want to thank my teacher, Ana. And my dad, who is here today, even though he’s gone very serious. Dad, don’t worry: I can draw bridges too.
“me hiciera ingeniero” = I became an engineer (imperf. subj.)
“se ha puesto serio” = has gone serious
El chico más callado del instituto
¿Qué le dice Andrei a su padre al final?
Andrei’s father was called Dan and he was a bridge engineer. He was a tall man of few words, who always wore the same grey jacket and looked at the world like a maths problem.
Ana met him on the day of the prize-giving. He was sitting in the back row with his arms crossed. When his son went up on stage, he didn’t clap. When Andrei mentioned him in his speech, he went pale.
At the end of the ceremony, Ana went over to say hello. Mr Dan shook her hand firmly, but he didn’t smile.
“You’ve filled his head with ideas,” he told her in surprisingly good Spanish. “Drawing isn’t a profession. You can’t pay for a house with drawings.”
Ana was left speechless. She didn’t know Andrei’s father spoke Spanish. Later she found out he had worked in Chile for five years, building a bridge in the Andes.
“I haven’t filled his head with anything,” Ana answered, trying not to get angry. “Your son already had all that inside him. I just gave him a pencil.”
Mr Dan looked at her for a moment. Then he turned and left without saying another word.
In the following weeks, Andrei went quiet again. He no longer stayed after class. He no longer left drawings on Ana’s desk. One day Ana asked him what was wrong.
“My dad says I have to give up drawing and study for the engineering exam,” he answered, looking at the floor. “He says I’ve become a dreamer and dreamers have nothing to eat.”
Ana didn’t know what to say. That evening, at home, she told Mihai.
“My dad wanted me to become an engineer too,” said Mihai, with Rosa Elena asleep on his chest. “He said doctors never have time for their families. It took him ten years to accept it.”
“The day I saved the life of a neighbour in the village. He realised my job built something too. Not bridges, but something.”
Ana had an idea. It was risky, but she couldn’t think of a better one.

The next day she spoke to the head teacher, Mrs Popescu. She suggested organising an exhibition of Andrei’s drawings at the school. Not of cats or paellas with legs, but on a specific theme: the bridges of Bucharest.
The head teacher thought about it. Then she smiled. “I think it’s an excellent idea. And I know someone at the town hall who would very much like to see it.”
Andrei worked on the drawings for a month. He crossed the city with his sketchbook: the bridges over the Dâmbovița, the metro viaducts, a nineteenth-century iron bridge that hardly anyone knew about.

But he didn’t draw them like an engineer. He drew them with people: an old woman walking her dog, two lovers kissing, a child throwing stones into the water. In his drawings, the bridges became places where life passed by.
The exhibition opened on a Thursday in November. Pupils, teachers, a few parents and a man from the town hall in a tie came. Mr Dan didn’t come.
Andrei watched the door all afternoon. Every time it opened, he tensed up. Every time it wasn’t his father, he got a little sadder.
At seven, when almost everyone had left, the door opened for the last time. It was Mr Dan, in his grey jacket, with his hair wet from the rain.
He didn’t greet anyone. He walked slowly round the room, drawing by drawing, with his hands in his pockets. He stopped in front of the last one: the nineteenth-century iron bridge.
In the drawing, on the bridge, there was a tall man in a grey jacket, holding a little boy’s hand. Underneath, Andrei had written: “The first bridge my dad showed me.”
Mr Dan stood still for a long time. Then he turned round. His eyes were red.
“He was four,” he said quietly. “I explained to him how the arches work. I didn’t think he’d remember.”
Andrei didn’t dare say anything. His father came over and, for the first time in a long while, put his hand on his shoulder.
“The arches are well drawn,” he said. “The proportions are perfect. You could become an architect. Architects draw… and they have something to eat too.”
Andrei burst out laughing and crying at the same time. The man from the town hall, who was standing nearby, came over with a business card in his hand.
“Excuse me for interrupting,” he said. “The city is going to restore that bridge next year. We’d like to use this drawing for the poster.”
That evening Ana got home soaked to the skin and happy. Mihai was waiting for her with a hot cup of tea.
“He came,” Ana answered, smiling. “And I think something in him has changed. He hasn’t become a different person. But he’s started to look at his son differently. Sometimes that’s enough.”
A few weeks later, the bridge poster appeared at bus stops all over the city. Under the drawing, in small letters, it said: “Illustration: Andrei Ionescu, aged 16.”
One morning, on her way to school, Ana saw Mr Dan standing in front of one of the posters. He wasn’t moving. He was wearing his grey jacket and holding his phone.
He was taking a photo. Then another. Then another, from a different angle, the way engineers do when they want to be sure something is well built.
Ana walked past him without saying anything. But when she reached the corner, she turned round. Mr Dan was still there, in front of the poster, smiling.
